title: The river looked holy… until God touched it.
paragraphs: The river looked holy… until God touched it.
Egypt built its life around the Nile.

The Nile was their economy.
Their agriculture.
Their survival.
Every year it flooded the land and left fertile soil. Crops grew. Families ate. Cities flourished. To the Egyptians, the Nile was not just water.
It was sacred.
They worshiped it. They trusted it. They believed their future flowed from that river.
But then one morning, the God of Israel confronted the illusion.
In Exodus 7, Moses and Aaron stand before Pharaoh again. The command had already been spoken:
“Let My people go, that they may serve Me.” (Exodus 7:16)
Pharaoh refused.

Not once.
Not twice.
But stubbornly, defiantly, repeatedly.
And so God began to dismantle Egypt’s pride—one plague at a time.
The first target?
The very thing they trusted most.
The Nile.
God told Moses:
“By this you shall know that I am the Lord: behold, with the staff that is in my hand I will strike the water that is in the Nile, and it shall turn into blood.” (Exodus 7:17)
And then it happened.
Aaron lifted the staff.
He struck the river.
And before the eyes of Pharaoh, his servants, and the people of Egypt—
the Nile turned to blood.
The water turned red.

Fish floated lifeless to the surface.
The smell of death filled the air.
The river that once sustained life became a river of decay.
The Scripture says:
“The fish in the Nile died, and the Nile stank, so that the Egyptians could not drink water from the Nile.” (Exodus 7:21)
Imagine the shock.
Mothers trying to scoop water for their children—only to see blood dripping through their fingers.
Farmers staring at the river they depended on.
Priests of Egyptian gods watching their sacred symbol collapse in front of them.
The Nile, their pride, their idol… was powerless.
This plague was not random.
It was surgical.
God was exposing the false gods of Egypt.

The Nile god Hapi.
The fertility gods they trusted.
The system of belief Pharaoh used to control the people.
One strike from the Lord—and the illusion shattered.
But here is the deeper truth:
Exodus is not just the story of Egypt.
It is the story of the human heart.
Because every generation has its own Nile.
Something we trust more than God.
Money.
Success.
Relationships.
Power.
Reputation.
Security.
We say we trust God… but deep down we cling to our own river.
And sometimes God allows the river to turn red—not to destroy us, but to wake us up.

When careers collapse.
When relationships break.
When plans fall apart.
It feels like judgment.
But often it is mercy.
Because idols never leave quietly.
God exposes them so we can see what we were really trusting.
And Pharaoh’s reaction in Exodus 7 is terrifyingly familiar.
Instead of humbling himself…
he hardened his heart.
The Bible says:
“Pharaoh’s heart remained hardened, and he would not listen to them, as the Lord had said.” (Exodus 7:22)
Even after seeing the miracle.
Even after the river turned to blood.
Even after the entire nation suffered.
Pharaoh walked back into his palace as if nothing had happened.
That is the danger of pride.
A hardened heart can stand in the middle of a miracle and still refuse to bow.
But the story does not end there.
Because the plagues were not only about judgment.
They were about revelation.
God was revealing something to Egypt, to Israel, and to every reader who would ever open the book of Exodus:
“You shall know that I am the Lord.”
The plagues dismantled false gods one by one.
But they also pointed forward to something greater.
Because centuries later, another moment of blood would change the world.
Not the blood of a river.
But the blood of a Savior.
Jesus Christ.
At the cross, God confronted the deepest plague of all—the plague of sin inside the human heart.
Our rebellion.
Our pride.
Our refusal to let God be God.
But instead of striking us with judgment…
Jesus took the judgment Himself.
The river turned to blood in Exodus as a warning.
But the blood of Christ flowed at Calvary as salvation.
Scripture says:
“In Him we have redemption through His blood, the forgiveness of sins.” (Ephesians 1:7)
Pharaoh hardened his heart.
But Jesus opened His hands.
Pharaoh clung to power.
But Jesus surrendered His life.
Pharaoh refused to let people go.
But Jesus came to set captives free.
And that is the question Exodus 7 leaves hanging in the air:
What is your Nile?
What are you trusting more than God?
Your success?
Your money?
Your influence?
Your plans?
Because anything we trust above God eventually becomes an idol.
And God loves us too much to let idols rule our lives.
So sometimes He touches the river.
Not to destroy us.
But to call us back.
Today the invitation is simple.
Do not harden your heart like Pharaoh.
Bow before the Lord.
Repent of the idols.
Trust the Savior who shed His blood so yours would not have to be the price.
Because the same God who turned the Nile to blood…
is the God who sent His Son to wash sinners clean.
And that is the hope of the Gospel.

📖 “Thus says the Lord, ‘By this you shall know that I am the Lord: behold, I will strike the water that is in the Nile, and it shall turn to blood.’”
— Exodus 7:17

God is still confronting idols.
And Jesus is still saving sinners.
